TASK GIVEN TO THE ENGINEER
ThreadSanitizer reports a data race when two connected QObjects that live in different threads
are destroyed in parallel: destroying the receiver calls into the sender while the sender may be
running its own destructors in its thread. QtNetwork triggers this on every HTTP request.

COMMIT MESSAGE OF THE REAL CHANGE
Fix data race on a sender's vptr when its receiver is destroyed

~QObject() resolves the signal and calls disconnectNotify() on each of
its senders. Both are virtual calls, so they are only safe from the
thread that owns the sender: any other thread may be running that
sender's destructors right now, which rewrite its vptr as they go.
ThreadSanitizer reports this for any two connected objects destroyed in
parallel, and QtNetwork hits it on every HTTP request.

Keep notifying inline when the sender belongs to this thread, and post
the notification to the sender's own thread otherwise, unless that thread
can no longer deliver events (e.g. it has finished). If the sender is
indeed being destroyed, ~QObjectPrivate() discards the event.

Fixes: QTBUG-133213

QBuffer tracks a counter up and down. But use of QBuffer outside of its own thread is probably a mistake, if not an outright bug, so I don't think that's a problem.

`QAbstractConnectionInterface` overrides the `disconnectNotify()` to be notified when a receiver disconnect and we no longer need to listen to the signal.
```
void QDBusAbstractInterface::disconnectNotify(const QMetaMethod &signal)
{
    // someone disconnecting from one of our signals
    Q_D(QDBusAbstractInterface);
    if (!d->isValid)
        return;

    // disconnection is just resource freeing, so it can be delayed;
    // let's do that later, after all the QObject mutexes have been unlocked.
    QCoreApplication::postEvent(this, new DisconnectRelayEvent(this, signal));
}
```
We could want to avoid double-posting of events, but we can't have zero events, which is the normal case when one disconnects from the interface's own thread.

QFutureWatcher base has code similar to QBuffer, but that one I don't know whether it could be used from outside its thread. But the worst case is that we have a delay in deciding whether to emit the `resultReadyAt()` calls. I don't think there's harm.
